projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Robert C. Cable was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Robert C. Cable. Robert served in the U.S. Army 17th Airborne Division. He served in the European Theater and his highest rank was corporal. I'm Tom Swope, and this recording was made at Mr. Cable's home in Middlefield, Ohio on October 3rd, 2001. Robert was 77 at the time of this recording. And you were living in this area when the war broke out? CABLE: During the war, I was living in Cleveland, Ohio.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Cleveland, okay. Drafted?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Drafted right into the Army. And they let me graduate from high school. I was just short an hour or two, so they said, When you graduate in June, and that would be 1943, you will immediately go in the Army. And they meant immediately. Seven days and I'm at Fort Hayes in Columbus, Ohio, which is sort of a distribution point for the Fifth Army. From there they sent me to Fort Bliss Texas, which was an antiaircraft outfit. And also there was a big field there -- they had it be an airport because we were basically antiaircraft. We would shoot down airplanes--was our primary job. And I had a gun crew and a director. One man pumped the lateral, one man pumped the vertical on the 40 millimeter cannon, which we could fire at low scraping airplanes even with that weapon. But then apparently they -- we got command of the skies, so we didn't need too much antiaircraft. They sent me to Texas to an infantry outfit where I immediately took a full course in infantry training. And they also sent me to some more schools. From there they sent me to Campon, California. Why I went to Campon, I have no idea. I think they were considering sending us to the South Pacific. But at the last moment things got more dire in Europe, so they shipped me to Campon, California where they then put me in cadre duty where I trained other soldiers in combat and in mines and demolition, chemical work there, judo, and judo bayonet fighting. For four months, I think, I was there. Then they decided they needed infantry men again, so they shipped me back to Fort Hood, Texas where I went through some more -- very little training. We were just there for a short period of time, and they decided we were going to Europe. So they sent me from there to Fort Meade, Maryland, which is a distribution point for going overseas in the European conflict. And from that point they sent me to Boston, Massachusetts where they put me on board the H.M.S. Moratinya (ph), which was a British ship, which was the sixth largest ship, I think, in the world at that time. Boy, there must have been 10,000 troops on that boat. That's what I heard. That's what they said, 10,000 people. We slept in bunks overneath our table where we ate. You stretched out your hammock right over your table where you ate. And we lived on candy bars because the British -- nothing against the British, but their food was horrible. All they had was that lamb and a boiled potato and a lamb with nothing but gristle on it. So it was a rough trip. We had good weather, missed a couple of--had a couple of submarine scares, but no problem. Then they took us all the way around to the other side of England and we landed at Liverpool. I assume maybe South Hampton couldn't handle a ship that big, I suppose. So they loaded us out of that, put us into little small British trains, shipped us in 24 hours--we didn't go very fast--across England in 24 hours to South Hampton where they put me on a boat in the English Channel. We had a couple of threats there of air strikes. The Germans still had some planes in the air, not many, but they -- this was before the Bulge, of course. So they put me on and I crossed the Channel to LaHavre, France. Got to LaHavre, France, they decided we were going to go to the nearest repo depo which was a replacement depot for the -- it was actually at that time the 25th or the 26th Infantry Division. Just for a short period of time. Then we left. So then we went to -- then they sent me to Belgium, which was a repo depo, a replacement depot. Then while we were there, an officer came down from the 17th Airborne. He said, We're looking for volunteers. I was 18 years old. We said, you know, that's not a bad deal. We get 50 bucks a month flight pay for that time. I think our base salary was 28 dollars a month at that time. 50 bucks was big bucks. I mean I was living off my mother for two years. So we liked that. First we didn't do it. We said, Oh the hell with it. Don't want it. Walking back to the apartments where we were staying, I look at him, he looks at me, and he says, You know, that doesn't sound too bad actually. Me neither, I said. Just something about it just seems right. So they put us on a truck. Took us to another point where we got on a C-46 or C-47. I think it was a 47 because they didn't use too many 46's as cargo planes, except the paratroopers jumped out of C-46's and 47's. They also towed our gliders. So we were quite familiar with that. Anyway, they flew us into Reims, France, where I joined the 17th Airborne. Now we're getting into the Bulge.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When did you land in France?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Oh, boy. Let's see.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Probably it was the fall of '44.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: It had to be, had to be. It was the worst Christmas I ever spent. It was the Christmas of '44.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That was the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Right, right. That started, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So it must have been a few months before that.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. I got a sheet in there that shows.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That shows you the chronology of things?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Yeah. I got it somewhere.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Don't mean to be rough on you? When did you join the 17th Airborne? About when was that?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: That would have been --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Shortly before the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Shortly before the Bulge, yeah, because I remember the weather conditions were atrocious. We were losing 2,000 men a day, not to combat so much as to the weather. I mean frozen feet, frozen fingers, everything. We had a lot of problems with that. And the Germans were -- of course, they stole some of our uniforms and they were all dressed in white. We had a lot of problems with identification because they could infiltrate our ranks and talk -- more German soldiers could talk English than English kids could speak German. Of course, they done that because they were going to conquer us. I mean, Adolf Hitler said that. So they would be able to speak English. You couldn't fool -- we couldn't fool them with the old Babe Ruth deal, you know. Nobody knew who Babe Ruth was. The german soldier was too clever for that. So they did a lot of infiltration, and sometimes we shot people just on an impulse because we didn't know for sure. It could be one of our own men. And what are you going to do? So anyways, then they were going to send us into -- well, right there was Bastion too because the 101st Airborne was trapped at Bastion and we were at Reims, France at that time. And they said that we're going to relieve the 101st Airborne. We loaded our gliders up, latched everything down. 2 a.m. in the morning and we are ready to take off on an air drop with our jumpers, and the gliders, into Bastion. They decided at the last moment, thanks to George Patton, General Patton and his Second Army Division were there. And, you know, he's quite a glory hound. You either loved or hated old Patton. I can still see him standing in that weapons carrier with his two pearl revolvers looking like King Tut on a shit island. A friend of mine was in the Second Army Division, so he -- of course, I admired Patton. He was a great man. Some people just really did admire him. Anyway, they decided at the last minute to send Patton instead. So they aborted our mission and sent the Second Army Division in there and they relieved the 101st. Then we came back to a staging area and were in that area preparing for the invasion of Germany. When they -- we stopped the Bulge. We stopped it. We knew we would. I mean the supply lines were just too far, just too long. They couldn't keep it up. So once we got them trapped there, we took so many prisoners. We had so many prisoners sometimes we had trouble controlling them. But that was better than us. But then from that point, then we went over the Rhine and landed at Wesel, Wesel, Germany. And from there we went right down the Rhine River to Essen, Dusseldorf, Aukin (ph) Cologne, Muenster. In fact, Muenster was probably our biggest action. The Germans would go into these apartment -- everything was brick in Germany, too, a lot of brick. And they would go into the basement of the first apartment, and we would shell them with our 57 millimeter and we'd chase them down to where they were popping in. They'd run underground to the next apartment building. Well, eventually they ran out of apartment buildings and we took them prisoners. The problem was it was 14 and 15 year old kids were involved. What do you do with them? They got guns. Sometimes they'd pick up a gun. Three kids accidentally got their hands on a German 88 millimeter, which was the best weapon in the war. There were no better weapons than the German's 88 millimeter. They could shoot planes out of the sky with it and attack an infantry division with it. That's how good they were with that 88. They said you could hit a fly at 900 yards. Anyway, -- I lost my train there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The kids got ahold of an 88.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Correct. And they accidentally -- now, we don't know if they fired it on purpose or they accidentally fired it. But anyway, we had three of our guys standing there and it hit right in the middle. Blew their heads off, blew them to smithereens. We got the kids and, of course, you know, we shot them. We didn't know -- there's not going to be any questions asked about this. You hate to do it but you have to do it. I opened up a door at one place -- I opened up the door, I had a -- the Thompson submachine gun I was carrying as a squad leader, and I raised my gun and he raised his. I held out my hand. I should have shot him. I held out my hand and he give me his weapon. Maybe if I had a brother who was killed like my other friend did, I would have probably shot him, too, 'cause he hated anybody because they killed his brother. So anyway, we got back there -- we got all the way down to Kuffadray (ph), Germany, which was a little town just below the Bavarian Alps where Adolf Hitler's Eagle Nest was, Berchtesgaden, and that's when the war ended. Shortly after that the Germans surrendered. And we were in this little town. They had me basically on occupational duty now, although the German citizens thought we were nuts. With Airborne you've got to get up at 5 o'clock in the morning and run 25 -- well, not 25, run five miles carrying a damn telephone pole. We loved it. We thought we were safe. But then if you had -- at that point when Germany surrendered if you had 80 points--which you got so many points for a Bronze Star or whatever--you could be discharged. Well, I had about 40 points, so did everybody else in the airborne units. Of course, the 82nd Airborne saw the most combat and they were replaced six times over in World War II. That doesn't mean they all were killed. But six times they replaced the compliment of men. Unbelievable. I'm having a little trouble with my up close memory in the last couple of years, Tom. I lose track of my thoughts. I'm known to correct myself, quite as well as in the past I did. But, hey, what can you do?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Let's see. Where were we at? We were in Kuffadray. We used to play soccer. They had a gym, a high school gym there, and we played soccer in that gym in our stocking feet. It was a nice slippery floor and we played hockey and soccer and all kind of games, basketball, had a net. Of course, when the German people saw us there, they thought we were nuts. We did one great thing in Kuffadray. We took over the leading liquor establishment in the town. We had our own bar. We sold the beer and whiskey to the Germans with their own money. They loved it. And we had no problem with it. We had very little problem with sabotage or very little problem with snipers at that time. Everybody was thrilled that the war was over for some people. But then we still had the Japanese. So all of a sudden we got our orders to move to Marseilles, France. All remnants of the 82nd Airborne, the 101st Airborne, the 17th Airborne and the 13th Airborne, all of us together under the auspices of the OSS because we were going to be sent in to do some strategic bombing and things like that to invade Japan. We were preparing for the invasion of Japan. Lord, I remember the ship. It was the Perfect S. Lykes, Jr. a Merchant Marine vessel that I was on. There were other ships there. I have no idea. I can't even remember -- I was more interested in playing baseball. We had a baseball team. We bet everybody, and we used to win money playing baseball. But I put down that the Perfect S. Lykes, Jr., which as I say, was a Merchant Marine vessel. And we were literally pulling out of that harbor on our way to Japan when Harry F. Truman dropped the atom bomb. I don't know if I told you, Tom. They turned my ship around and sent me back to New York City to the Statue of Liberty. I'm still not out of it. I'm in Marseilles, France now. But then when Harry dropped that atom bomb and sent us back home, I've been a Democrat ever since. Sorry to say it, but what else could you do, right, Tom?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: So they sent me back to the states. I can still see coming into New York Harbor and the Statue of Liberty. From there they sent me to Fort Bragg, North Carolina. From Fort Bragg they sent me to Fort Benning, Georgia to the airborne camp at Fort Benning. And then from there they sent me to Indianapolis, Indiana which was where the separation center was for the Fifth Army. Then they gave me my discharge then and there. It was kind of an odyssey of -- I can't say that we were lucky, the 17th Airborne. We saw some combat but certainly anybody who missed D Day -- I mean D Day that's combat. That's the real combat. It's fake but sill that's the real -- that's the way it is. Although showing -- like when they show a hand grenade as blowing up a jeep and two weapons carrier -- I mean a hand grenade sometimes it won't even kill the person that's holding it. I mean it's not that big. But everything is big to them, I mean, if they are all setting off bombs. And then they do Private Ryan. You know, after a while you don't really care about war movies. Now they sicken me. It is such an obscene act to send 18 and 20 year old kids to their death. Eisenhower groped(?) with that problem in England in 1944. He was -- he knew what he had to do and yet he had a little problem accepting it, and I can see why because it is so unnecessary. Now as you get older, I mean, war doesn't fascinate you any more.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were a squad leader. Were you a squad leader the whole time there?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Yeah. Even when I was at the 821st Antiaircraft Unit in Fort Bliss, Texas. I was there -- in the army six weeks and they made me a PFC. I thought, wow, the way I'm going, I'll be a general by the time -- and then they made me a corporal because I was a squad leader and in charge of the gun. At that time, as I say, I was on the directory which is a machine that followed the plane and gave you distances and then I would give the--like 1500 yards to the gunner and the gunner would automatically move it in to the target that I picked out the range for. And as I said, one man would crank the vertical and one cranked the horizontal, plus we had two guys hauling ammunition. Plus you had somebody taking away the debris, too. So -- and, yeah, I was the squad leader there too. When I got in the 17th Airborne with my background, they immediately put me in charge of a six-man 57 millimeter antitank weapon. And also I -- on occasion they moved me up to the 90 millimeter. And we had the 50 caliber machine gun mounted on the jeep. And there was another weapon we used quite -- with some degree of success. But our combat experience was fortunate. With all the zooms I'd gone through, they are all fraught with danger. I mean I dropped -- B-2 rockets are falling out of the sky. B-24's crashing. Like I said to Franky Baker, I said, God knows how many times I saw you flying over Germany and France at that period of time. He flew 57 missions. Died in a fire at his house over here in -- he lived in Willoboughy Hills. We used to go to the breakfast club. We had breakfast together once a month or once a week with Franky. I knew some of his family as a kid.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: As a squad leader overseas then, what was your job?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Same thing. Basically same thing.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were in charge of how many?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Had six. Mainly I had the 57 millimeter antitank weapons, was what I had at that time. That was big enough. What we knew it was perfect. That was a good vessel, a good weapon you could use against the type of combat we were in, apartments, blowing people out of apartments and taking prisoners. Oh, God, we had so many prisoners. And that one fellow I was telling you about that hated the Germans so much, he would hold out the stock of his rifle as they was going by, these Germans, and whack them in the head, which we didn't appreciate. I mean I understood why he done it, but -- or his hate. War teaches hate. And don't tell me about men, women and children. It's sad if you think you can have a war and protect all the innocent, good luck. We're getting in a situation like that now, I guess. Boy, think twice before you start sending people over there. I don't know. What do you do, Tom?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, you talked about Truman. Do you remember the day FDR died?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. We were in -- let's see. Were we in Kuffadray already or were we still like at Muenster? We spent three or four days at Muenster, which is a little smaller city but it just happened to be an area where the Germans were congregating. One reason they were there too is because they had a big hospital. This hospital, it's got the flag, you know what I mean, the Red Cross on it. It is well marked. Totally marked. We knew it was a hospital. We didn't touch it with a ten foot pole. It was German, too. The Germans got in there and set up their command post in the hospital and started firing at us from the hospital. So what can we do? We fired back. They lost a lot of their people. But they were desperate. I mean it was -- the war was winding down. So many Germans, too, would say that when we met them and we would take them back as a prisoner. They'd say, The mean old Nazi, mean old Nazi, mean old Nazi. Oh, yeah. There wasn't a lot of Nazis in Germany. Right afterwards when I came back from overseas and they said that there were 9 million members of the Nazi party. Now, Germany at that time was 60 million people, so that's about a tenth of the people. So actually most of them were non-Nazis. We didn't realize it at the time, but whatever. They were excellent. They did not do crazy things like the Japanese or these terrorists today. I mean they are willing to die. Our people aren't that willing to die. We will if we have to. But they don't care. They are so dangerous because they don't care about life. They think they are really going to Allah. They believe it. We don't give -- yeah, maybe. Why not? Sure. Not like them. They believe it. That's why they are so dangerous.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you ever have to do any landing with a glider?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I made three tactical landings, which is back behind the lines. And then -- on a Rhine River crossing our glider was aborted at the last moment and we crashed -- we didn't crash, but we went down because the Germans had detected where we were going in. The Germans had their 88's lined up. They were shooting -- they were shooting us out of the sky like -- and there was no necessity for it. I mean we could walk across the Rhine. I mean the Germans were not that -- even though this one particular spot was bad. But they aborted a lot of them. They aborted more and more. I mean even aborting them, you get credit for going over the Rhine and all that crap. But it was for our benefit. I mean it was ridiculous to send 10 gliders, not like sending in ten flight squadrons to get one fly. And then even when we landed in Wesel Germany, when we got into Wesel, Germany we had to connect up with the British Second Army Division. If we didn't connect up with the British Second Army Division, we were in trouble because we only had food for three days, ammo for three days and that's it. And we could not take any prisoners. In that first invasion when we stepped on German soil, for whatever reason, for the paratroopers, the glider or whatever it was, once we set foot there -- what am I saying? Lost my track, I guess.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wesel, Germany.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Yeah. Once we set foot off, we could not take prisoners at that particular point because I mean we are surrounded by the enemy supposedly. We were surrounded but fortunately they're not strong enough to make really an impression. The war was over. You just hated to get killed at that particular time. Unfortunately, and as I say, our biggest danger was in the crazy kids who believed in it. Some of them did, they fought. I mean they believed in it and they fought and they shot and we shot them back. Once we got in there, we can't horse around. We don't take prisoners. We shoot them. They shoot prisoners. You cannot take them. You can't -- fortunately for the Germans we felt they -- we had such control that we didn't have to be quite as beastly as we would be in another situation. In an airborne unit you are isolated. You go into enemy territory. You don't -- you're not going to land five feet away and walk in. You are going right into the enemy territory. So you've got to be prepared to deal with it. If you have really a strong enemy, there's other places to go. But in that initial foothold you've got nobody. Nobody is sacred. It's -- that's war. Nobody ever said it was supposed to be nice. This nice war and this comradeship and this heroism that we see on TV. Just like can you imagine the army sending ten guys in to save one private? Come on now. We wouldn't -- maybe we'd send ten privates into save one, but not send ten guys to save one private. No way, no way. So the whole premise of this movie is bad. Now Tom Hanks is doing another one, The Band Of Brothers. Did you see any of those, Tom?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I didn't see any of those.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: I don't care to. I haven't -- I did watch D Day way back. Let's see, that was June 1944. Let's see. I was in California. We went all the way through France, fighting in France. I had a friend who was in the Big Red One in France. He saw a lot of country. The infantry -- there's only one problem. The infantry? The artillery man? They're back. Everybody's back. The generals are all back. You don't -- no marking -- there was never any marking to show an officer to the enemy or anything. You don't wear anything shiny either.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have any close buddies? Got stories about close buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Yeah. Even some that -- no. I guess because we -- at that particular point, the 17th Airborne was manned by people like me who did not -- they were formed in Fort Benning, Georgia, in 1942 I think. And they were sent to England. The 17th Airborne was in England at the very time I was crossing England to go to South Hampton. The 17th Airborne was still in England at that time. And we thought they were going -- the rumor was, and I wasn't even with them then, but the rumor was that the 17th Airborne was preparing for the invasion--for the D Day invasion. They didn't use the 17th Airborne in the D Day invasion that I know of. I can't remember. They were still in England. They had to have some backup. But they had like 500,000 troops massed in that -- all the armies are there; the British army, the French army, the -- whatever remnants of the Italian army that were with us. They were all -- there were several armies there. I have no idea how many. And the 17th was still there. And then when I went from the Harbor, we went to the repo depo in Belgium and was there for several days with the 17th Airborne -- but they no longer had to have an airborne invasion. They just came across the channel and swam away as an infantry unit and went up into Belgium and then down into Reims, France and that's when I joined them then. So we had a lot of new people because they lost -- I say it's amazing how many people we are losing and yet we're winning the battle but it was mostly the weather. I think the weather had just -- it was just -- some people were more susceptible to that. I had clean socks. I mean I stood up in a foxhole one night, 20 degrees temperature, frozen to the skin, artillery shells all around us, people yelling. And they said, Just don't leave this area. We've got to protect this sector. The Germans are going to counterattack. Well, we were by a canal. I mean, it's cold. Damn, I don't know why every time you want to fight a war you have to get up in the morning. I say if you're going to fight a war, let's start at high noon. Why get up at 2 a.m. in the morning to die? But that's the way it is, Tom. But I mean it's scary and cold. And you don't -- how -- why I didn't get -- maybe I was just young. We were in good shape. Our generation, we lived on the farm. We knew how to walk. We knew how to hike. We weren't fat. We knew mainly how to shoot. I had a gun when I was nine years old. On a farm that was nothing. I mean like we had an 80 acre farm in North Bloomfield. I didn't hit anybody. I mean I could set off the atom bomb and not hit anybody. But -- so we could fire weapons. We knew how to shoot. I mean I shot -- I could shoot a crow in the wing with a .22 rifle. That's how -- I mean I was no Super Man, but we all could--we could do those things. Things like that make a good military man.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why don't you describe how a glider works, the whole process here? You hook it up to what?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: A C-46 or a C-47. Now, in Germany we used the C-47's. In the South Pacific they used C-46's. They were also used to transport troops too, and also the jumpers all jumped out of C-46's and C-47's. The jumpers worked in conjunction with the gliders, of course. And the paratroopers wanted nothing to do with the gliders. They -- near the end of the war they said, Everybody in the airborne unit is going to be both paratrooper and glider. And you people who have your parachute badges have to get ready for glider training. You people in glider training can get ready for paratrooper training. And they had the towers. 250, 300, 400 foot towers. That was your first jump. You jumped off of that just to see what the weight of a body will do and ride the ropes when you -- when the parachute opens up. That's primarily what that was. But the glider, we had to do that, too. I did jump off one tower, and then the Bulge became more immediate and they stopped all of our training and put us immediately back into combat in the Bulge area. So we went back into combat at that particular time so I never finished, thank God. I didn't particularly care about -- but they were safer. There's no doubt the paratroopers had a less casualty rate than the gliders. It was just no -- anyway in the glider, like I say, we could carry -- even sometimes a weapon. But the biggest thing we ever carried I think was a weapons carrier, which is a small truck. Then we carried a jeep on one glider with a 57 millimeter. You know about that. And then the 57 millimeter antitank weapon was in the glider, too, plus the equipment and your ammunition and five or six troopers. Not too many troopers in there. And a pilot and a co-pilot. Now, the pilots and the co-pilots when that glider landed or jumped -- of course, they didn't ever use the airports with the gliders. We had to have a man -- they could be steered and flown. They had pylons just like everything else. So everything was -- like the floorboards were not--were plywood. They was mostly piping, metal piping, that kept it together. I mean you could stick your foot through the side of it and the wings. There's an awful lot of flying that way. Every now and then a wing did fall off. It had so much weight. It's not a glider. It is not a glider. It's just to get that thing. It makes a circle twice and lands. It's got to land. There ain't no where to go. And if there are 9,000 Germans there, or there's all types of asparagus--they called it Rommel's asparagus, which were the spiked things they stuck in the ground to ensnarl the gliders when they landed. You didn't need too much for that. But -- and they were loaded from the front end by lifting up the front end. And they loaded -- let's see. What else did they have there? And then, of course, the tow plane was a C -- what did I say? In Europe we was using the C-47 and then you would -- they had the tow rope which was loose, and they would just take off and they went to pull us. Two gliders too because of a certain ________the more they get in the air the better. So each C-46 or 47 carried two gliders which was heavily loaded, now, too. And there was nothing -- you had -- everybody said, Well, you had parachutes. No, no. There's no parachutes for glider troopers. You're never going to use that. You can't do anything about it. I mean you can't shoot from it if you go down. There's no way you can fire from that glider while you are landing, and you wouldn't. There's not really much you could hit. There's nothing to shoot at. So there's not much there. And then when the glider gets up, of course you are at the mercy of the pilot and the co-pilot. If the pilot and the co-pilot sees something that is totally disastrous, he may abort the mission. He may land the glider and release it. He dropped the tow rope. When he dropped the tow rope, the glider is on its own. Even if the glider pilot said to the C-47 pilot, I don't want to be aborted, if the pilot -- and you got the pilot of the plane, too. He's got to watch out because they shoot him down, too. In fact, he's a nice target going 120 miles an hour towing two gliders. What else did we have in there? Oh, yeah, they had wheels on them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: That's a riot. They could leave the wheels. You can see it -- but here, that's a slide. That's what it landed on. Forget the wheels. I mean if you were in a real--like an air base where they -- one time they took us up at an air base, they took us up in a glider, dropped it and landed it. Took us up again, dropped it and landed it just to give us the idea of the feeling of it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So either the pilot of the C-47 or the glider pilot could release the tow line?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Yes, right. And the pilot for the gliders came from usually Air Force guys that got kicked out for something. We had a colonel drive one of our gliders. He was really bad. He scraped the tower -- the tower at the air base where we were staying. That wasn't so bad that he scraped it with a B-24, that big plane, but he was drunk at the time. So they give him two choices. In those days they gave you two choices if you could fly a glider. If you can fly a glider, you can become a glider trooper. Which if you become a trooper, now, forget that pilot stuff. When it lands you're combat, you're infantry. Or you can go back to the--we'll send you back as a private, ship your ass somewhere away. So most of them stayed 'cause not everybody was -- everybody thought, Oh, ain't nothing to a glider. Most airplanes had a bad time. You could move your air lines and steer the thing. They did have a glider, and they do have it at the Air Force Museum. Have you ever been there?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: They moved it. Last time I was there they hung it from the ceiling. Well, if everybody keeps walking through there -- that's a fact, though, Tom, they can barely hold up with that because if everybody starts walking through these gliders and doing things -- that's the only one they've got left, I guess.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It is?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: That's the impression I had. Yeah. I took my kids there, the grandkids there. They wanted to see the glider, but it's -- first time I saw it, that's right, the first time I saw it it was on the ground. You could walk through it and look at it and see the controls. But after that they hung the damn thing from the ceiling because they were afraid it was going to be destroyed by -- just like at Yosemite and they say, How did they wear out the rocks? The spectators, the people going through there. That's the basic glider information.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did they remain intact when they landed if they didn't hit anything?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Yeah. Some of them did just barely, because they would circle twice and then land. If they come in at a fairly decent area, yeah, they got a chance of landing it. Some chance, not too much. But there is a -- of course, the Germans where very good too at placing their defenses. They knew pretty well, just like we knew pretty well, what they were doing, too. Everybody said, Why did Eisenhower wait? why did he -- we had the Germans on the run, which is true. We had them on the run. All we had to do was hit them one more time and knock 'em out. Eisenhower was out of gas. 10,000 gallons of gas a day he needs to run them tanks. And who brings it up? The biggest heroes of the war are the truckers who drive -- bring all that equipment up to the front lines. And they get shot at, too. They were the real heroes because there's no other way to get there, by plane or by truck. So that's why the Red Ball Express, they call them, they ran 24 hours a day delivering fuel. So he couldn't do anything about it. And the Germans were aware of that. That's another reason why they probably initiated the Bulge at that time. They knew this was their last gasp at any -- what they wanted was a better peace. They knew they were not going to win the war. They wanted a better peace, a better term, than they would have got otherwise.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about that experience over there, what comes to mind as your most vivid memory?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: I guess the most vivid memory, I seen this man standing next to me smoking a cigarette with half his face gone and he's standing there smoking a cigarette. And it was one time when we got hit by some artillery fire which we weren't expecting at all. And that -- but the whole place was fraught with danger. I mean you got that time two young girls, 14, 15 years old. We always went -- whenever we went anywhere -- even at the replacement depot you weren't safe. We always traveled in pairs. We were walking back to our apartment house one day and bang. I hear two shots and two slugs hit the wall right above our head. Fortunately we were right close to the building where we lived and we went in there. We sent our people out. Any time we got there we went out the back. I think they found the two girls, too. I'm not sure but we heard some stories about that afterwards. They'll find them but they may be in a -- we'd shoot them. If we knew they had a weapon and the weapon was hot and it had been fired, even though we couldn't identify them. If you're in the vicinity with a gun, you're dead. That was the closest I come to being hit--a at repo depo. But in combat itself when we were at Muenster Germany, the Germans had -- their 20 millimeter cannons had a real orangey tracer. No. Theirs were blue and ours was red. And this blue tracer they fired -- and you'd be laying on the ground and you would swear that tracer is going to take your head off. In fact, I had a back pack on -- that that's the closest I came to a Purple Heart. Had my back pack on and probably was a 20 millimeter shell hit a tree or something right close by and splattered and tore my pack off my back. And in it was a picture of Judy in there and there were indentations all over her picture, which she still has it. And that was the closest I came to a Purple Heart. But the Germans, they -- at that time they had a good weapon. Their 20 millimeter was a fine weapon. They were very accurate with it. Fortunately for us though there just wasn't that many of them anymore and we had superiority. That's probably the -- of course, that's a vivid memory. But there are others. I think going into New York Harbor and looking at the Statue of Liberty after that odyssey I'd made. All those places I stopped. I guess we're getting near to covering all of them. In fact, that's what I wrote down here. I don't know how many -- we covered all of them--most of the places where I was at.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were married at the time?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: No, thank God.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember getting letters and that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Oh, sure. Oh, yeah. Judy and I wrote back and forth. She thought -- one time I said, I'm not concerned about getting married at this point. She thought I meant I may never be. It wasn't because of the war. Just 'cause I didn't want to, but it wasn't because of the war. I felt so excited -- I was just so lucky. Where I was at my timing was just perfect to have missed D Day 'cause I had the age. My age was perfect. I'd've been there. And with my background I'm sure I would have been there if they would have -- so we lucked out there. But the married guys, I thought there was something wrong with me sexually. I thought, What the hell? These married guys, Jesus Christ. I gottta go in town and get laid tonight. I used to laugh and say, What the hell? I mean I'm 19. What the hell? I don't know anything about nothing. Well, that was it. I didn't have any steady diet of sex. These poor married guys, 34 -- and plus that they were out of shape. I mean I was so young. I couldn't get out of shape yet. I mean we were so lucky to be -- because they suffered so much. And I mean being away from their family and kids. You know, what the biggest revelation was? That when we went through the pockets of the German dead looking for information about their ship movement and you pulled out his picture of him and his two little kiddies. I can't talk about that too much.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Personal things like baby pictures?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Yeah. It just made you think, garrrr. He's just like you. We're all alike. What a horrible thing to inflict on anybody. Thank God my son didn't have to go to war. He missed Vietnam with my (inaudible). No way I said if -- and they said go -- you go to college, you know, we're not going to draft you. Well, of course, he went to college. He was going to go anyway. It worked out great. None of my grand children, I didn't want to see them in that either. Believe me, if we live long enough, Tom. When I think about that, all the walking -- I guess that's why men have a little problem with longevity over the women because the men--our bodies are brutalized a little bit more by walking, combat, running -- (loud noise) Gee, was that a terrorist?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I hope not.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Air raid siren?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (Laughs)

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Yeah. Thank God, none of them have to go, huh, Tom?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm. So what kind of things did your girlfriend write to you?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Like basics. We weren't -- at that particular time we had only met each other once or twice. And I made that trip from California, from Campon back to Cleveland twice. That wasn't exactly fun. And that's another memory. Sitting up in a car full of -- I know these trains always had coal dust. There was always coal. You felt coal dust in your coffee. We stopped at the USO's every time we stopped at a little town even like Helen, Montana. I remember that because Helen, Montana was the hometown of Gary Cooper. And it had mud streets. It had no sidewalks at that time, Helen, Montana, up in no man's land. And when you sat up in that train for three days and four night, or four days and three nights, whatever it was, from making that trip from there to Cleveland, you were -- there was not much left, Tom. I always thought -- and you always went through Chicago. We'd stop there on my way back to Cleveland. Going back there, we'd get home -- and my dad was World War I. And, of course, we belonged to the VFW Post 1500 which was in east Cleveland then, because we lived on 128th and St. Clair at that time when Judy and I was first married. When I went in the army, I was from 128th Street. After the war when we got out there and looked at the school systems there, we said, No way are we going to send our kids to school here, so we moved out in the boondocks. Of course, we're both farmers. Our generation were -- now, I didn't -- my mother and father didn't make a living at the farm. They tried to but they couldn't make it. But my grandparents did. Went to my grandparents -- where were you going to go? It's 1930. This is going back a little bit, but this is the greatest generation -- why Brokaw calls us the greatest generation and he's right. For going through the depression and from that point on we went into World War II. We come out of the depression, here's World War II. Of course, I thought everybody was in the same boat we were. I thought everybody had trouble finding -- on a farm, at least you ate. But we were on relief. We had to come to Cleveland and we had to get relief to pay our rent. My dad was trying to get a job and things were so difficult.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember where you were on Pearl Harbor day?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Yeah. It was on a Sunday. We were home. We lived 128th Street when that happened, yeah, Pearl Harbor. And Bob Feller immediately volunteered and the Indians were devastated. They could have got him off. Most of the ballplayers got off anyway because they said entertaining troops was part of their job. And I would -- we had -- the 17th Airborne had a battalion team. We didn't have a division team at that time, but we had a battalion team. I played on that. I played -- my best baseball was played in the Army, and I was probably, what, 20 or 21. But, yeah, we were home. It was Sunday and we were home when that happened. Of course I was about, what, 16? I didn't think it was going to involve me at that point. Everybody said, Oh, it'll be a quick war. We'll knock 'em out in 20 minutes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you know what Pearl Harbor was?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You did know that?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: A lot of guys I've talked to they said they had no idea.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you knew where Hawaii was?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, yeah. Hawaiian, yeah. Of course, that's a very meaningful day to us. But that was so simple. Everything was so simple. We knew the enemy. We had no doubts about that. And the Germans had they invaded England when they should've in 1940, God only knows what would have happened. We'd've had no base in England. He would have conquered them, no doubt about it. He didn't listen to Rommel, fortunately for us, huh?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Exactly. Well, (inaudible) Russia wasn't very brave.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Hell, no. Yeah. And to me the Russians spent, what, eight years trying to capture Afghanistan and trying to do damage. They never could. The Afghanistans ran them out. They never could. That was their Vietnam.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Afghanistan. Although the Russians now are coming around, I think. They are more -- they may be in our corner now finally.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You think they may be?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Yeah. We need 'em. That's for sure.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your home coming when you actually got back from overseas and saw your family for the first time?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Yeah. You know, some of that is such a blur, Tom. I'd have to really think hard on it. Like I said, once we got through the Statue of Liberty, I mean it was--to go back home again, to be alive. I guess you didn't even think about -- you know, when you're 18, 19 you don't think about immortality. You don't have no -- you have no concept -- that's why
(END OF TRACK ONE)
(BEGIN TRACK TWO)

in the military, I don't care whether it was in combat or where he was at, paid his dues. I know it was all -- not only was it dangerous, but your life style is so changed, everything is changed, everything is taken away from you at the moment. I think probably the worst part, and I can't blame anybody for it, it's nobody's fault, is that you can't talk about this to anybody but another veteran. Other people don't understand. They just don't understand. They look at these motion pictures and think how glorious war is and chivalrous. I mean it's one thing with a man standing with his arm blown off. I mean it happened so fast, like that kid told you about. I mean, he's smoking a cigarette. It happened so fast. You don't even know enough to fall down. You're dead and you don't even know it. This is a man I met. Judy loved it because that's General Stakofsky, the first parachute--Polish parachute battalion. He was at Reims, France with us, his group. They had those Polish guys. They were the pick of the litter. They were all six-foot-two, 200 pounds. Good outfit. Done a good job. They were in that Market Square deal. That's the one where what's his name the British general? Newton -- Montgomery, Field Marshall Montgomery.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: That was his idea. Said we -- Cornelius Ryan wrote a book about it called A Bridge Too Far.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Bridge Too Far.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: And they got caught up in that, too. We were not involved in that. That was way ahead of us. Like the 101st and 82nd was involved. The 413th Airborne, 413th, they were south of us when we went over the Rhine. And before anybody could do anything, Patton sent his tanks across the Rhine. Had his engineer there, loaded up, against orders, he went across the Rhine. So the 13th Airborne lost out. But he was lucky.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: He saved a lot of lives in the long run because if they had sent -- they'd never been in a combat situation with gliders at all. That would be their first and only. And he died in an unfortunate accident.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I know.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: He was yapping so much about the Russians that they knew -- we knew we could not go into World War III at that point. Nobody in their right mind, they know we can't do it because we got to, Hey, keep it low key here. We've got a nice Cold War going here. We can build some more ships and stuff. Build another aircraft carrier we don't need.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: That's another ballgame. I have trouble talking about him. I had a cousin, Jerry Cable, who was a -- Jerry was always a free spirit. Anything going on, he'd be right there. You needed a volunteer, he'd be the guy. When World War I started, that was 1940 already, he joined -- well, it was before World War I. He joined the -- because he knew it was coming. He knew it. There were a lot of people that did. And he joined the Canadian Air Force and flew in and got his wings as a Canadian. Then when Briton went into the war first, he fought on the side of the British as a Canadian and flew several -- he flew the P-47 Thunderbolt through several missions.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (Inaudible__+)

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Because we were so close. Anyway, and then he fought for that. He was in North Africa. And then he got shot down. That was after he had gone through the Canadian, the British, and now he's in the -- in fact, at Pearl Harbor he joined the American Air Force. So he's in the American Air Force.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: He used to come to Cleveland, oh, back, when I was 11 or 12 years old. He was like probably 10 years older than me, because if I was 13, he'd be like 23. We were very close. He was a trucker. He'd come into town with his big tractor and we'd go all over the place, to ballgames, to the movies driving his big tractor. He'd park it. He didn't worry about that. He'd done dropped his load off at the terminal. And then him and I would go bumming around. Sometimes he would say, Okay, Bob, I got to leave early today. You go on home. Here's car fare to go home. You know how to get there. He made sure I got to the street car stop. So I went home. And whenever he came into town, he'd call me. So we done this for quite a few years. He was married and divorced. Never had any kids or nothing. He loved being a trucker because it was freedom. He wouldn't care. If he knew he was going to die, he would've still done it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (Inaudible ___+ skipping?)

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Where we got so much of it, when the Germans evacuated an area they left all their gun pits. Well, we'd come charging in there, why build another gun pit? We've got theirs.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: But we found out after we had a few accidents -- we knew every time we went into a -- that was my job. I had a crew and I went in there -- what we would do with our bayonet, you'd take your bayonet and you'd go -- we'd all lay in a row and cover a certain area like three of us could cover, and then we could start at the left. One, two, three, four, until somebody hit metal. Then when you hit metal, then we cleared the debries around that because then they had an anti device on that which would set off the whole thing. So if you deactivated the small -- what am I saying? First you had to make sure there was nothing under -- usually it was a land mine or a tank mine. And then you'd have to clean away the dirt and look underneath it to find either a trip wire or a pressure point before you stepped in it and we could deactivate it. I mean, we knew most of the mines the Germans used. We knew about them. Every now and then they'd put a ring around it. Every now and then they'd put what appeared to be a mine and nothing there, but a couple of feet away they'd put -- if you hit the trip wire, it sets off another bomb. So you have to watch for trip wires, the big bombs and then the little tiny things that set them off. What do you call them? I went to school for that. All those years -- blew all the skin off my thumb once. We used to use that big heavy fire cracker in training. That's what we used in training. And if you set that, it would go off just like anything else. And if it did, you're dead. But you could lose a finger or two. Nobody liked it. It sounded bad, but I don't know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They're trying to train you, right?

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: We just done it. I said, You're going to do what? You want me to do what? We're too smart now, Tom.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I hope. (inaudible__+)

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: We were out in the desert in El Paso, Texas there in that Mojave -- Mojave? Anyway, the desert. We were out on maneuvers and we were on infantry maneuvers. We'd run and the officer would yell, Duck. Well, you had to look for the nearest spot to hide behind, a rock, tree or whatever. And if you didn't, he'd come tap you on the shoulder, You're dead. You're dead. You're dead. You see that rock? What are you doing here? There's nothing here. So, Tom, I'm running and I see this indentation. I give a big leap forward. Something stopped me. I don't know what it was, like you said some --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Here it was, a sunken mine shaft. We'd drop stones down there and we couldn't hear them hit.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Whoa.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: I went down there. You're a dead duck. I came inches, slight inches -- that wasn't even in a combat area. You want to talk about heat in Texas? I went down to Texas in June when they sent me to Fort Bliss. It must've been 109 in the shade.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: (Laughs)

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: We got off of that train and they lined us up in front of the train, and I heard this plop, plop, plop. What the hell is that? I look around. Here's guys fainting. The heat was so -- why it didn't bother me, I don't know. I mean it bothered me, but I didn't pass out. So there again, most of the guys that passed out were older.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert C. Cable
sp.p: Younger guys don't pass out like that. The heat was so oppressive. That was one of the worst moments for some of the guys.
